subtopic: MOBILIZATION OF CANADA'S RESOURCES- REPRESENTATIONS OF CANADIAN LEGION
speechtext:
Could the minister of National War Services make a statement with regard to the coordination of the activities of the many war charities now carrying on in this country? Perhaps before he answers that question I might make one or two observations.
Splendid work is being done by the many women's organizations, who give of their time, energy and money to a most remarkable degree. But it does seem in many cases that they do not have sufficient guidance as to the results of their efforts, or as to whether they are doing the most economical and most satisfactory type of work. For example, only a day or two ago Miss Macphail, formerly a member of this house, made the statement in the press that ladies in the district around the town of Durham, I think it was, might better be employed making children's dresses instead of knitting socks, which can be turned out by machinery so much more quickly and more cheaply than they can be knit by hand. In Toronto the same condition exists. I wonder if the minister's department could not indicate to these organizations the sort of work they might do to the best advantage. If there were someone in each district as a regional officer, if you will, charged with responsibility directly from the department, who could find out from the department the type of work that might be done to best advantage, it would be of considerable help. Even if that information could be circulated in the press it would be of some assistance.

The War-War Services
There is another point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. In most areas this work is carried on by groups of ladies who congregate in church basements, private homes, or, as in the case of Toronto, in vacant store properties, which they turn into a sort of headquarters. Perhaps the minister's department might give some consideration to this suggestion. Where a store property has been turned over to an organization of this kind, entirely without charge, could the owner be exempted from payment of income tax on the amount of property tax he has to pay on that building, or even to the extent of the carrying charges on the property? If that could be done I believe many desirable centres would be opened up in various communities where this work could be carried on in a much more efficient manner. Then there is the further point that when these groups meet in private homes there is a tendency on the part of many people to entertain perhaps a little extravagantly. If these activities could be organized more efficiently much better results might be achieved.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. T. THORSON (Minister of National War Services):
subtopic: MOBILIZATION OF CANADA'S RESOURCES- REPRESENTATIONS OF CANADIAN LEGION
speechtext:
When I first appeared before the committee I referred in a very general way to some of the points which have been mentioned by the hon. member for Danforth, and at that time indicated that my department was coming to the view that the time had arrived when we did not wish any increase in the number of war charities or in the number of war activities of a charitable nature, but that we were hoping that the men and women of Canada would give consideration, in respect of their various war charities, to the coordination of their efforts rather than to any expansion of the field of activity.
As hon. members are aware, every application for permission to engage in a war charity must be made to the war charities division of my department in order that a permit may issue under the provisions of the War Charities Act. Every application for such a permit is carefully considered by the officers of the department before a permit for the registration of a war charity is granted under the provisions of that act. There are a number of activities which are of a more spectacular nature, shall I say, than others. Certain activities make a very attractive appeal to the men and women who are engaged in them,
but it does not necessarily follow that these activities are the most desirable, or that the men and women taking part in them are thereby making their greatest contribution. If I were to make one general observation in reply to the question asked by my hon. friend it would be this, that the men and women of Canada should get behind the great national drive that will take place in the spring of 1942. I refer to the joint drive in which the great national war auxiliary services organizations will take part, and in which the Canadian Red Cross society also will participate. I could discuss the activities of these services, but the general observation I would make would be that instead of multiplying the number of separate activities of this kind, the men and women of Canada might well get behind the national drive that is to take place this coming spring.
The national war auxiliary services organizations such as the Canadian Legion, the Knights of Columbus, The Salvation Army, the Y.M.C.A., the Y.W.C.A., and another which is going to take part in the next drive, the Navy League of Canada, are in the main performing auxiliary services for our troops both in Canada and abroad. On the other hand the Red Cross society is performing its splendid services in accordance with its traditional position as an instrument of mercy in time of war. Its activities have been tremendously increased. Up to recently, for example, it was packing 10,000 parcels a week for prisoners of war. That activity has been increased to 35,000 parcels per week. In addition, it is engaged in activities of a nature which give aid to the bombed [DOT] victims of Great Britain.	It has been performing a
splendid service in its blood donor arrangements. All these activities are of a great and humane kind. The operations of such an organization deserve the support of every man and woman in Canada, and I should like to see the men and women of Canada who are anxious to make some kind of contribution to the war effort make it in that field and in support of that drive, rather than in a multiplication of war charities of one kind and another. I shall have more to say about the national drive later when we have fixed upon the date and our plans for its success are further advanced.
I do take this opportunity however to urge upon the men and women of Canada that
The War-War Services

they must make an absolute one hundred per cent success of the approaching drive. It will be a large one, in the field from $17,000,000 to $20,000,000. That is a large amount of money, but the Canadian people have never failed to respond to a single appeal that has been made thus far, and I devoutly hope- indeed, I know-that they will not fail to respond in this instance.

subtopic: MOBILIZATION OF CANADA'S RESOURCES- REPRESENTATIONS OF CANADIAN LEGION
speechtext: As the minister has pointed out, these moneys are pretty well regulated and governed by the government. It arranges for the work to be done by the organizations to which he has referred. Since it is work to aid our soldiers, could the money not be taken from the national revenue rather than through a national drive? The people are heavily taxed and regulated as it is; could we not avoid the canvassing which is done repeatedly across the country? With all the safeguards and regulations enforced by the government on the expenditure of this money, which is to be used for the assistance of our troops, it strikes me it would be better to take the money out of the national revenue.

subtopic: MOBILIZATION OF CANADA'S RESOURCES- REPRESENTATIONS OF CANADIAN LEGION
speechtext: No, that is not my view. It may be necessary for the government to undertake the financing of some of the auxiliary services now rendered to our troops by the national organizations I mentioned a moment ago. I am definitely of the opinion, however, that there is a tremendous value in having the thousands of men and women identified with these organizations engaged in the task of assisting in the auxiliary services. The services of the Red Cross, by reason of its inherent nature, must be voluntary. So far as the auxiliary services are concerned, I see a great advantage in having thousands of men and women across Canada actively associating themselves with the promotion of these services to our troops. It would be much easier for the auxiliary service organizations to get their money direct from the treasury, but I am satisfied the country would lose something of incalculable value if this voluntary effort were replaced by putting the whole burden on the federal treasury.

One finds it very much on the prairies where there are numbers of alien farmers whose sons are not enlisting, and I believe this condition is proving very harmful to recruiting. Surely when a person comes to this country and gets all the advantages of Canadian citizenship he should be prepared to accept the responsibilities involved. We are told that only the young men who pass the physical tests and are placed in category A are called up under the mobilization act. If these young men who pass as category A are called up and are later found not to be physically fit, are they put in a lower category and retained in the army? Assuming the answer is yes, I submit that is

unfair and irregular. If a young man is called up, and does not pass the tests, he is not in the army, but if a young man is accepted and eventually is put in a lower category, he is in the army. So that one man in category B may be in the army while a thousand other men in category B, of the same age, are not in the army. Let us not fool ourselves; of course, we have conscription in Canada to-day for home defence. Everyone knows that. But if we are going to conscript some in certain categories and leave others of the same age and the same category not conscripted, it is unfair and I would say highly irregular.

Members of the denomination of Christians called Mennonites and members of the community of Doukhobors who immigrated to Canada pursuant to the arrangements evidenced by the order in council of August 13, 1873, and by the order in council of December 6, 1898, respectively, or the descendants of such immigrants who have continued without interruption to be members of the aforesaid sect or denomination of Christians or of the aforesaid

That may be a low attitude to take; it is not a loyal attitude, but nevertheless the feeling is there. It would seem that the government was trying to save face when Mr. Justice Davis called all members of the house together to discuss this war service act. On that occasion I said, "Are there any exemptions?" And he replied, "No; there are no exemptions under the act." Finally he did say, "There are exemptions from war services for Doukhobors and Men-nonites." The feeling went out through the country that this was unfair. The thousands of young Mennonites and Doukhobors born in Canada enjoy all the privileges of entering industry-because they certainly do not all stay on the farms. They receive good wages, and they are exempt from war service, not because of any law on our books, but because the administration says, "We will consider the same law applies to them as applied to their parents and grandparents, when they came out here."
The government then said, "Here is what we will do: we will take them into camp we will show the people of Canada that these Mennonites and Doukhobors are to be conscripted"-not to fight for the country, but to build more roads so that tourists may drive over them years hence. It is a profitless waste of energy and money. In the county of Waterloo and the surrounding district, young Mennonites have been taken off the farms, and they have been told by the government, "You are not to be conscripted for war service." All right if that is the government's attitude, we will abide by it. But those boys have been taken off the farms and sent to the camps to build roads-useless roads-while the crops have been left lying in the fields. We cannot get exemption for those men. It is a strange policy. It seems that we want more food and are telling the farmers to produce it, but in order to save the face of the government, in connection with granting exemption to those who, under an old agreement, ought not to be entitled to it, these men are being taken off the farms and sent into camps to build useless roads while the crops lie wasting in the fields. I know of farmers working 200, 225 or 250 acres of land. A man holding an acreage of that size, and doing mixed farming, has a great deal of work to do. He would have 20, 25 or 30 head of cattle to milk every day, and certainly he could not do it alone. Some of those farmers are selling their herds and giving up their farms. Pick up any weekly paper and we find that there are more auction sales on farms to-day, in the third year of the war, than there were during the depression. Those farms are being sold, not because the farmers could not make farming pay if they were given an opportunity, but because the government is taking the men off the farms and sending them to do useless work.

Perhaps we ought to get down to earth in this matter and distribute the work according to the jobs the men are going to do, so that we may have better service than we are now getting.

The experience of Great Britain in the last war with regard to conscientious objectors was an unfortunate one. At the beginning they did not recognize that viewpoint, which to perhaps all of us is an incomprehensible one, and they filled Dartmouth prison to overflowing with conscientious objectors. Anyone who has made a study of the unfortunate experience of the British government with conscientious objectors in the last war will realize the lessons that were learned by that government as a result, and they have not in this war repeated the experience. There is one matter I want to bring to the attention of the minister before he rises-and I suppose he is hoping he will rise pretty soon; I know that another minister is anxious to get on, and I want to help-and it has reference to the travel bureau. Then, passing from that, I should like to refer for a moment to the present position of the Canadian travel bureau. When this bureau was established in 1934, it was attached to the Department of Railways and Canals, which subsequently became the ministry of transport. There it remained until the present Minister of National War Services was appointed to his portfolio, and then, for reasons which appear to me to be not very logical, it was transferred to the present minister. I am not suggesting that the present minister is not qualified to handle the work of this
The War-War Services

bureau as the political head, but I do suggest that, as the ministry of national war services is essentially a war department, the transfer of this peace-time bureau to a war department was psychologically a mistake. That is my first submission. I do not believe-and I have heard this view expressed by those better qualified to judge the matter than I am-that the travel bureau should be associated with a war department. They have nothing in common. I suggest to the minister that the tourist industry has suffered greatly since the very outbreak of the war from propaganda which has been spread in the United States in the attempt to keep their nationals within their own territory, to the effect that tourist activities in Canada may be and are interfered with as a result of this country being at war. Fantastic stories are reported to me to have been spread in the United States, to the effect that, "If you come up to Canada, your car will be taken away from you", and also that "you will be conscripted." Those responsible for those stories have an ulterior motive, namely, they want to keep their tourists in their own country; and the very fact that Canada is at war and that the operation of this bureau is under a war service ministry has had a distinct effect in keeping out of Canada people who are desirable tourists. I believe that the association of the bureau with this ministry lends credence to the fantastic views which have been expressed in the United States.
I have here a letter from the travel bureau. It is entitled, "Canadian Government Travel Bureau, Ottawa, Canada. Department of National War Services." That is on the letterhead. I assume that hundreds or even thousands of these letterheads go to the United States. Thereby the government is disseminating information among would-be tourists in that country that the travel bureau is a war service. There is an association of ideas which we just cannot get away from; it is wrong, and it has had a detrimental effect on the tourist bureau.
I suggest to the minister, not with any intention of disparaging his activities or his capabilities, that this travel bureau should be dissociated altogether from the idea of war services and be put into the Department of Trade and Commerce, or somewhere else, so that this bad psychological effect may be obviated. There is no doubt that we want these people to come into Canada. There is no doubt that the coming of the normal number of tourists into Canada would be a great help to us in connection with the foreign exchange problem.

By the same token the restrictions on the issue of Canadian currency for travel in the United States have had a bad effect upon the reciprocal action of United States nationals coming into this country. If the minister wants any confirmation of that, I would ask him to consult with our Canadian minister at Washington; I think he has views on the subject. I have no authority to quote him, but I suggest that the minister find out what our highest ranking official in the United States has to say about this matter, and then see if something cannot be done. I am satisfied that if there were greater provision for Canadians to visit the United States and mingle with the people there, they could become good missionaries for Canada, enlightening the United States public as to Canada's war effort, and there would not be the slurs that we sometimes hear and read as to Canada's war effort.
I offer these suggestions in good faith. As long as the Canadian travel bureau is associated with a war service, that fact will be used by those who have ulterior motives, and the very object for which parliament is voting money, namely, getting United States tourists into this country, will be defeated. I commend this suggestion to the minister with all the earnestness at my command: let him- get the tourist bureau out of his department, get it into Trade and Commerce or some other department, so that the wrong impression will not be drawn by those who want to draw wrong impressions for an ulterior purpose. Do not let the minister forget to ask the Canadian minister at Washington what he thinks about this interchange of travel. We cannot have it a one-way business. If we want tourists to come to Canada, ten to one, fifty to one perhaps, spending money in amounts relative to their numbers, on balance we shall be ahead notwithstanding the opinion of the foreign exchange control board.

come up for some discussion. One is the bureau of public information and the other the matter of salvage. I am not entirely satisfied that the bureau of public information is making the very best of its possibilities. We call it a bureau of public information; it could well be called a bureau or ministry of propaganda, for, after all, that is what it does. I believe we have a good deal to learn as to more effective methods of propaganda. The bureau of public information has been giving out a good deal of information concerning Canada's war effort. That is all acceptable, and I suppose there is some reason for the people being informed as to what Canada is doing. But from the point of view of propaganda, from the point of view of stirring up the public, it seems to me that a little more attention might be given to the nearness of the dangers presented by the enemy. Perhaps we have to be a little more definite and specific with certain information.
I attended a theatre the other day, though it is not very often I do so. There was a newsreel shown on the screen, and when a picture was shown of the President of the United States delivering an address I could not help thinking what a powerful piece of propaganda that was. He said something to this effect: "I have before me a map of the western hemisphere which has been obtained by the intelligence branch of our government. On it appear specific plans for nazi aggression, for the occupation of south and central America." I said to myself, "that is powerful stuff." I think we could be a little more powerful along similar lines. The raft of material put out by the bureau of public information does not seem to me always to click. We read about certain appointments being made; a certain individual has been appointed to a certain position. Then his biography is given. He was born in a certain place, in England or some other country; he obtained his public school training here and there, and all the rest of it, and I doubt very much whether the people care where he came from or what he knows. As the hon. member behind me says, they are more anxious to know where he is going than where he came from.

When I say that, I am going to suggest that journalism is a very highly specialized profession. A journalist is not merely one who can write good English, or articles of perfect composition. That will amount to a good deal of money, and it seems unfortunate that such an expenditure should be necessary when we realize that the work was done previously by voluntary help.
There have been occasions when salvage collectors have done wonderful work, but when very little return has come from that work. In some instances they could not even get rid of the scrap. The result has been that the enthusiasm has died down. My suggestion is that the government is entirely to blame for this state of affairs. I have in mind a particular incident which took place at High River, Alberta. I hold in my hand an excerpt from the High River Times, which reads as follows:
Sale From Scrap Iron Returns -a Sad Story
Net proceeds salvage drive brings $29.93 to bombed babies; railway gets $243.36 for hauling
Never was so much done for so little
Theme song on elevator row "we've been working for the railway." Donors swell chorus
The sum realized out of the scrap iron collected by the High River elevator agents from farms of the district, has brought $29.93 to the fund in -aid of bombed families of Britain. There

The War-War Services
were 31 tons assembled and shipped out by railway from this point. The freight charges on the shipment to Winnipeg were $243.36.
This net result of all the labour on behalf of the refugee fund, has set the elevator agents, the contributing farmers and other donors back on their heels. The letter of appreciation from the Patriotic Salvage Corps at Winnipeg, acknowledges the receipt of the $29.93, as "the net proceeds of the carload of scrap metal." The same letter congratulates the agents on their splendid work, and suggests that they now go after the salvaging of rags in the district.
Just ask the boys who sweated over the scrapiron, how soon before they are going to start after rags, and you may get a black-eye out of it. It is safe to say they won't start immediately. Never was salvaging enthusiasm at lower ebb amongst these patriotic citizens.
The letter received from the Patriotic Salvage Corps attempts to shed a little brightness by saying, "While in view of the total value of the metal shipped, the net proceeds of $29.93, appears very' small, we must bear in mind that freight charges from your point to Winnipeg are extremely high, and in this case amounted to about $250. However, there is one compensating feature of this shipment and that is that you have made available for the defence industry a very much needed shipment of raw material."
It is realized grimly that if the scrap had been trucked up to Calgary (even if they had paid $1 a ton for trucking) the refugee fund would have been boosted by $200 or more. But the instructions were to ship to Winnipeg as the headquarters for the disposal of the metal.
It is doubtful if history can record such small net result from such an amount of combined labour, cheerfully and generously given. Every person participating, including the seven elevator agents, 35 or 40 farmers, two or three truckmen and a wrecker from town (and one musn't overlook free publicity in the Times) - all of these gave something of commercial value in material, time, labour, transportation or news space. Incidentally some pretty good clothing was also worn out in the cause. This was given mainly out of sympathy for the fund for bombed families. All this, to raise the sum of $29.93.
In the letter the minister sent out on October 20, he used the expression, "although we have been unsuccessful in obtaining any concession from the railways".
We are going out again to ask the farmers to contribute scrap metal. We are going to ask them to give their labour for nothing, and to give organizers well over S3,000 to organize those campaigns. We shall have instances like those we had before. In reply to the question: "Is the Department of Munitions and Supply in need of the steel produced from the scrap metals so collected?", the minister said, in the return filed:
The chairman of the war-time industries control board and the steel controller, Department of Munitions and Supply, advise that scrap iron and steel in all forms is urgently required.
I assume that is correct. When I spike on this matter last year one of my chief concerns was that of obtaining scrap steel for our war effort. On that occasion the Minister of Munitions and Supply told me definitely that his department did not need the steel produced from that scrap metal. Only the other day I had a call from an organizer asking me to go out to help him collect. I am not going to waste my time, or that of the people in my constituency, for nothing. If the scrap metal is needed, our attitude will be entirely different; but I want to have the question settled.
No longer ago than June 11, 1941, as reported at page 3812 of Hansard, the Minister of Munitions and Supply stated definitely that his department did not need the steel produced from that scrap metal. I was amazed that this was the condition, and it will be recalled that I was one, and only one, of those hon. members who persisted in having the Calgary rolling mills opened, in order to have that scrap steel handled. A short time ago I visited those rolling mills to see how the work was progressing. Well, I saw. I could not help this morning contrasting what I saw in the moving picture made available to us by the minister's department-or possibly one of the other departments. I refer to that moving picture showing the English people working day and night, not even stopping for meals, on account of the urgent need for guns. They did not take time off for dinner; it was brought to them. The plants were operating twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. There was no whistle blowing and no time off for lunch periods. I suppose that this scrap iron is urgently needed.

Mr. Chairman, I believe a question of privilege is in order at any time. I have just seen in the evening edition of the Ottawa Journal an article headed:
No Conscription Under Mr. King Caucus Told.
Premier Discussed Problem with Winston Churchill.
This is a communication by the British United Press, and the first paragraph reads as follows:
Prime Minister Mackenzie King told a Liberal caucus last week that so long as he was head of the government there would he no conscription in Canada, it was learned on highly reliable authority to-day.
Another paragraph further on reads:
Informants said that Mr. King had told his followers that he discussed the problem of conscription with Prime Minister Winston Churchill during his visit to Great Britain. The effect of his conversations with the British Prime Minister was to confirm his own view that Canada, a country of less than 12,000,000 people was consequently limited in its available manpower for military purposes, the Prime Minister was quoted as telling Liberals.
While it is not customary to disclose matters that are discussed in caucus, speaking in the presence of members of the party who were present at that Liberal caucus I wish to say at once that I never mentioned the name of Mr. Churchill in connection with any discussion on conscription at any party caucus held at any time. The statement is false and, what is more, I believe it has been inserted not with a view to helping Canada's war effort but to make the war effort of Canada as embarrassing as it can be made at this time. I think an

The War-War Services
apology is due from the British United Press for publishing a statement of that kind before inquiring of the Prime Minister whether or not the statement was correct, I cannot protest too strongly against a misrepresentation that could not be grosser than the one appearing here.
There has been a great deal of talk lately about conscription. I want to make perfectly clear what is in my mind when I speak of conscription so that there will be no misunderstanding as to my attitude in relation to it. So far as conscription stands for compulsory selective national service, that is a principle which this government has embodied in its _ National Resources Mobilization Act passed at a previous session of this parliament. As to how rapidly that principle should be applied and how far it should be extended is a matter which the government must decide and will decide in the light of all the knowledge which it has with respect to the needs of our war effort and the position of the country in meeting them.
I want it to be distinctly understood that so far as the principle of compulsory selective national service is concerned for Canada, in Canada, I stand for that principle. I have never taken any other stand. It is the position that I have held all along. It has been applied in connection with military training and applied in a number of other directions I might mention. How much further it will be applied the house will learn as the government takes its decisions on that matter.
But so far as conscription for service overseas is concerned in the armed1 forces of Canada, that question was submitted to the people of Canada at the last general election, an election which was held in war-time, and in which the leaders of all political parties made their statements to the electorate, and the people of Canada decided against conscription for overseas service. So far as I am concerned, without any consultation of the people on that subject, I do not intend to take the responsibility of supporting any policy of conscription for service overseas.

The next question is:
3.	We should like to know from the minister the result of the recruiting campaign of June and July, and the results of the monthly recruiting campaigns, and specifically:
(a) the method by which the quota for the general recruiting campaign and for the monthly campaign was settled. Was it based on population figures in a given military district?
The answer is: Recruiting campaign: 32,434 required, 34,625 enlisted. Approximately 48,000 offered themselves for service.
In answer to (a), before I deal in detail with the method adopted in the general recruiting campaign, the following general observations may be helpful.
The mobilization scheme was based upon the structure of the non-permanent active militia for obvious reasons, the chief being that this organization was capable of the speediest expansion. Experience of the last war in connection with records and maintenance of continuity of the non-permanent active militia units made adoption of this scheme advisable. In mobilizing the non-permanent active militia units for active service due regard was paid to equitable territorial distribution, consistent with the availability of the arm or branch of the service required.
The objective of the campaign was 32,434, of which a portion was to bring units up to strength, and the balance as reinforcements for existing active units, including deficiencies of previous quotas. Only ten per cent of the above figure was for infantry, and the remainder for the technical branches, such as artillery, engineers, et cetera. These latter are mostly English-speaking and require a large proportion of tradesmen. Accordingly, whilst regard is had to estimated population in fixing quotas, it was necessary in the last campaign to take into consideration the geographical origin of the units to be strengthened or reinforced and the location of their reserve counterparts, as well as the availability of tradesmen and suitable personnel for the various purposes for which they were required.

I think it is my duty to try to throw a little light upon the matter brought up by the leader of the opposition, which the acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Power) has attempted to explain. Recruiting in New Brunswick has been based more upon geography than anything else. The oldest infantry regiment in the province, the York and Carleton Regiment, recruited for the first division. Naturally those who were already in the ranks of this regiment were among the first to sign up with the colours. It just happened that this regiment was recruited largely along the banks of the St. John river. Then recruits were taken from Madawaska, Victoria, Carleton, York and Charlotte. Those living in the Frenchspeaking section of Madawaska and Victoria counties naturally joined up with that regiment. Before the regiment was recruited to full strength, I believe a campaign was carried on in the counties of Restigouche and Gloucester. The number recruited from these sections was quite limited, but they helped to fill the ranks of the York and Carleton Regiment, first division.
When the second division was mobilized, men from the districts along the north shore formed the nucleus of the recruits in the infantry division from New Brunswick. More recruits were obtained from the northern or French-speaking section of New Brunswick than when the first division was mobilized. At that time, however, a number of boys who lived adjacent to the province of Quebec had enlisted in the Gaspe and Matapedia valley regiment which had been mobilized for the first division. Credit for those enlistments was not given to New Brunswick. These boys were French-speaking and they joined up with Quebec regiments.
In connection with the physical condition of those who joined, it is an unfortunate fact that the men from the northern section of New Brunswick were not as physically fit as those from the lower part of the province. I shall not attempt to explain this, but there are two main causes. These people have to work hard for a living. Many of them are engaged in lumbering, and they do not have much time for sports and games. They work from daybreak to sundown. Many of them are fishermen, and the life of a fisherman does not tend to produce a strong and robust man. Social workers will tell you that people who spend most of their time in a fog on the high seas, who are not working as strenuously as a farmer and who, therefore, do not require the same nourishment, do not tend to develop bodily to the same extent. Furthermore, they do not have time to practise physical culture, to go to doctors, and to carry out modem methods of hygiene. The war will have one good effect: it will enable us to remedy this condition as quickly as possible.

The Minister of National Defence put the situation with regard to recruiting very clearly last Wednesday. Referring to the recruiting campaign in the summer he is reported at page 4115 of Hansard as follows:
The assumption was that if we could enlist men at the rate of 12,000 or more per month in the campaign, there ought to be no difficulty in enlisting 7,000 or 8,000 under the influence of the momentum which had been generated. But there was a definite falling off. As the figures show, in the last four months, since the campaign, we have asked for 37,000 odd, and something over 24,000 have actually enlisted.
This means that the recruiting campaign at the present time is not a success, and that is

perhaps the most vital question facing this house at the present time. I would ask the minister to tell us what plans the government have in mind to make recruiting a success. We should be told what plans are in mind.
I should like to make two suggestions, and no doubt there are many others that could be put forward. First, it seems foolish to rely largely upon sending around bands all the time. I do not know what the practice is in other parts of Canada, but in Vancouver a band parades up and down the street two or three times a day, and there is a recruiting station or perhaps several of them. I think it would be much better if, in addition, we could have stationed in the city a tank or some other type of the most modem military equipment. I am quite sure that it would be of interest to our young men because they are all mechanically-minded anyway, and the army is continually calling for mechanics and tradesmen. I suggest that it would be very much worth while to change the present method and send some modern tanks to different parts of the country to give the young lads a chance to examine them and see how they go. In that way far more enthusiasm would be stirred up than is aroused at the present time.
My other suggestion is this. I think the government misses a grand opportunity by not doing something without further delay with respect to dependents allowances. When the war broke out the policy was adopted of paying an allowance for only two children of the enlisted soldier, no matter how many children he actually had. We were told at the time that it was done in order that men with more than two children would not enlist. But despite that fact, men were taken on who had more than two children, and there are many men in the forces now who have more than two children, yet their wives receive an allowance for two children only. I daresay nothing does more to hamper recruiting than to have that condition exist to-day all across this land. Here is the wufe of a soldier with five children drawing only the allowance that goes to the wife with two children. Not only is there bound to .be insufficient food for the family, but they cannot get proper living accommodation or proper medical treatment, and it is almost impossible for the family to live under decent conditions unless they have other means. I am sure that practically every member of the house has run into that difficulty, and I suggest that provision should be made at once to pay an allowance for all the dependents of a man who is overseas.
Furthermore, I think these dependents should get a cost of living bonus. As it is

The War-Air Services
to-day, they are pretty well forced to live on a minimum scale, which is not good enough for the dependents of the men of the fighting forces. I suggest that these women and children should be granted a cost of living bonus. The same applies to the men of the last war who are on war veterans' allowance, and to the pensioners, who are in a most difficult position. The young man who has not enlisted sees these veterans of the last war and says to himself, "Well, if I enlist, am I to be treated in that cavalier fashion when I come back from this war? What is the use? Why should I enlist and have to come back and fight the government in order to be able to live?" Those are the arguments with which we are being met in the ridings day after day. These men should get the cost of living bonus. Old age pensioners are in the same category. They are drawing only $20 a month and that simply means semi-starvation. They are on the government payroll just the same as civil servants, and yet, although they are given an extremely small amount to live on, they are not considered in the cost of living bonus scheme at all. Things like that are hurting the recruiting campaign, and until the government wakes up and realizes that these are the conditions across Canada to-day, do not expect very much in the way of recruiting. The government cannot get the men unless it remedies these conditions, and I urge that there should be no further delay in meeting them.

This is, perhaps, an unusual opportunity-to be able to direct a remark to the minister to-night in both his capacities, upon this subject of recruiting. I should like to mention to him one matter which has caused a good deal of heart-burning, and to make a recommendation in connection with it.
The high percentage of rejections through medical examinations is due to either one of two things. Either the national health of the country and particularly of our young men is more deplorable than I think it is, or a wrong emphasis is being placed on the system of medical examination. We are in the unique position-I speak now of the army, of which I know, not of the air force and the navy-that the Canadian Army is a creation of the medical profession, that profession being composed of people who understand the art and practice of healing and on that account are entitled to respect. But this profession is in the rather odd position, not of its own choosing, of saying who shall serve and who shall not serve, with the result that, I believe, a great many of these medical officers, being young men without practical knowledge of what is required of the service in its various branches, are forced to decide whether or not a man shall serve, according to a routine order and a little book, a book which anyone who has been turned down for service will probably remember having seen. It is not, I say, of the medical profession's own choosing, and it seems to me and to many others in the service that the time has come when recruits should be examined by soldiers, their capabilities assessed and the decision made as to where in the varied services of the Canadian Army they would most likely be valuable, and then, when that has been

decided, the medical officer should be called in to perform his true function, that of an expert witness who, having been told what is required of the particular man in the service for which he is destined, can state whether the recruit is physically fit for it or not.
Some of my colleagues may quarrel with that point of view, but I doubt very much if it will be seriously objected to by any of the medical profession. Under present conditions, in my opinion, there is wastage. I come back to the point I mentioned last night, namely, that we are judging every one of our prospective soldiers by the highest standard which would be required of any of them. In an army which comprises even six divisions or less, there is a place for those who, being willing and anxious to serve, do not qualify by the highest standards.
I put this suggestion to those of us who cheered when we heard the then Prime Minister of Australia say in this chamber:
What does it matter if we come out into that wmrld bankrupt? What does it matter if we come out into that world with lower standards of material living than wre have now? What does it matter if in that world the rich are not so rich? What does it matter if in the last resort the business of statesmanship in that new -world becomes the business of sharing justly a new and honourable poverty?
We cheered that; did we subscribe to it? We gave at least lip-service to it. But I suggest to the minister and the government that our attitude with respect to the substandard eases is prompted at least in part by the thought of the pensions yet to come. At any rate, I should like to see a reconsideration of the system of medical examinations.
Before I leave the subject, may I suggest to the Minister of National Defence for Air that the problem of recruiting, in so far as it is a problem, has been bedevilled somewhat by that which is in the nature of a contest between the services. I am one of those who think that recruits for all branches of the service might well be pooled and then, according to their various qualifications, assigned to that branch for which they are best fitted. Perhaps I would not give even the volunteers who come from our training scheme quite as much latitude in that respect as they already enjoy. I can understand the Minister of National Defence for Air getting enthusiastic about the fine body of men he has. We are all equally proud of them; most of us have boasted about his air force, and-some of us-about his own part in creating it. Perhaps he will not take it as unfriendly if I say to him that, in the opinion of at least one member of this house, it does not lie in his mouth to assert the superior Canadianism of any group of men in service in Canada, even the men in the force

of which he is so proud. I suggest to him-I think he agrees with me-remembering those men who serve in the army under less happy conditions, in particular, though not so much recently, still to some extent in the matter of pay, and certainly in matters of comfort, including the comical clothes in which we train our soldiers-that perhaps the test of sincerity of Canadianism and loyalty in the service was laid down long ago by One who said, "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life." I believe that the Canadianism of the men in the rougher khaki will stand the test, even though some of them may have to pass out without "benefit of matriculation."

Following what the hon. member for Vancouver South has said as to the necessity of removing all sources of dissatisfaction among service and ex-service men, there is a matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the committee, arising from a letter which I received this evening since coming into the chamber. I am going to read all material portions of the letter, which is from Earl Grey, Saskatchewan, and dated November 10, 1941:
I have received a letter from the Department of Pensions and National Health, together with income tax forms, and I enclose their letter which is self-explanatory, and which I thought you might like to read, the forms I am returning, completed, to the proper department.
I find it difficult however to reconcile the government's action in taxing the soldiers' pensions, especially when, owing to the increased cost of living, bonuses are now being paid to workers who are earning at least $25 a month more than my pension of $75 a month.
And this particularly, Mr. Chairman:
My pension is for the total loss of sight in the last war, and this handicap, which necessitates paying out for everything that is needed by me, is an added burden to the increased cost of living.
In the last session I made an appeal-and I know it was sympathetically received, although not acted upon-that pensions should not be subject to income tax. Up until the present time they have not been subject to the national defence tax. Attached to the letter is a notice received by this pensioner, a letter that apparently has been sent out to all pensioners in Canada, which reads as follows:
To all pensioners whom it concerns:
Subject: National defence tax.
A ruling given by the Department of National Revenue, income tax department, some months ago, to the effect that total disability pension was not regarded as income and therefore not subject to national defence tax has now been repealed.
I do not know the meaning of the word "repealed" there. The ruling in effect until recently was apparently that these men who are to-day receiving pensions by reason of the last war for total disability should not have imposed upon them the national defence tax. The word used is that that ruling has now been "repealed". I presume the word meant is "revoked".
It has been ascertained that there is no statutory authority in the Income War Tax Act for the exemption from the provisions of such act of total disability pension.
In the circumstances, this department will be obliged to make the necessary tax deduction from pension commencing January 1, 1942, in all cases where this action is indicated.
At a time when we are endeavouring to get recruits and every effort is being put forward to that end, even now at the end of this session we ought, in the interests of these men who to-day are in receipt of total disability pensions for their services in the last war, to remove that cause of dissatisfaction. I suggest that the act should be amended at once if there is any doubt, as apparently there is, whether the income war tax act provides for such exemption.

May I commend the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) for bringing up one matter which is near to my own heart. Nevertheless I would not have it thought for a moment that the interest which he has shown in soldiers' dependents is confined to the group to which he belongs. The sentiment is widespread not only in, but outside parliament, that an increased allowance of some kind should be made to the wives and children of soldiers who are in the army, whether abroad or still in Canada. The amount undertaken to be paid to the dependents of soldiers was calculated in 1939, and no doubt was calculated with care in order to give a living allowance at that time. If it was the right amount at that time-and I do not say it was or was not, but let us assume it was-it is the wrong amount now, because in the meantime the cost of living has advanced an amount which it is hard to state. It is easy to look up the cost of living index and see that it has risen 10, 15, 20, or 30 per cent; a little over 14 per cent is perhaps the general figure, but that figure is not quite applicable, because the style of living of these people is special, and one would have to calculate food and clothing specially and make due allowance for the kind of houses they live in and the rents they pay. The cost of living to them has probably increased more than it has in a general way. The likelihood is that the amount we are now
The War-Air Services

paying to them has decreased in buying power by more than 15 per cent over what was paid to them in 1939. I want to associate myself strongly with what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver South in the interests of these poor people. We have had representations made here in Ottawa as to children without shoes, children improperly and insufficiently clothed, and most important of all, children who are not receiving sufficient nourishment, who are underfed. That should not take place in Canada.
I have thought that one of the really statesmanlike conceptions which has passed into actual law in the last two and a half years while we have been at war is the cost of living bonus. I think the Minister of Labour is to be commended for that very sound provision which raises wages proportionately to the increase in the cost of living, and which will probably in due season decrease the remuneration as the cost of living falls. That is a statesmanlike provision and has had a marvellous effect in our industrial centres, because it has removed the fear that increases in the cost of living would so whittle down the standards of life that our people would be in a much worse condition than they are now or have been. It has removed fear, and in doing so has settled the minds of the people, and they have gone to work forgetting for the moment about their financial troubles. It would do the same with regard to the dependents of the soldiers if they knew that as the cost of living increases in the future, payments would be made to them increased proportionately with the increase in the cost of living. There would be found very much less discussion of this matter; these women would take care of their children, look after their homes, devote themselves to their domestic duties instead of feeling impelled to take part in public movements to save their standards of living.
I am glad to learn from the minister that a decision on that matter will probably come down in the near future. I hope it will be a favourable decision, and I would say a generous decision would be welcomed by the people of Canada. It would be a statesmanlike provision if a cost of living bonus is paid to these dependents. I took part with the city council when the matter was brought up in Toronto; I came down with the delegation to press it upon the government; I have taken every possible occasion of a private nature to advocate this measure, and I want it to be written in the records of this house that I am in favour of it. I hope not only that a favourable decision will be made with regard to the soldiers' dependents, but that

this bonus will be extended to all those people who are dependent upon the government for set amounts, so that the fear of the increasing cost of living shall be removed. They will know that no matter how high it goes, compensation will be given to them. The name of the minister who signs that recommendation will be blessed in this country.

I wish to make one or two observations in support of what has been said with regard to granting adequate allowances to soldiers' dependents. I do not think there is anything that would add more to the morale of our troops than to know that their dependents at home are being looked after. I do not know of anything that would stimulate recruiting more than to know that if our boys enlist their dependents will be adequately looked after.
I want to give two examples which have come to my notice in talking this matter over with my constituents. I have had several cases of boys who enlisted expecting to get an allowance for their mothers. In one instance this has been denied the mother, for the reason that she is not living with her husband. They are not legally separated; they have been living apart for many years; yet, because she has a husband living, she is denied the allowance in respect of her son who has volunteered his life in defence of his country. As I say, I have had several cases of that kind.
Then there is another instance I should like to cite to the committee. This is the case of two old age pensioners, each receiving $15 a month. They have a little property, which has been willed to the son who is now overseas fighting for Canada, who served during the last war and who volunteered once more for active service. I am informed by these old people that in the course of two or three years their equity in this little house will pass to the old age pension board, and I was asked if it would be possible to have the Old Age Pensions Act amended so that in such cases, where the son enlisted, the board would not exercise the lien which it held on the property.
I want to submit that case to the acting minister to-night. About a week ago I wrote a letter concerning this particular case to the Department of National Defence. I do not know whether that letter has come to his attention, but I should be glad if he wrould give careful and favourable consideration to the two matters I have submitted.

I want to assure the minister that in the part of the countiy from which I come the situation has been terrible for the past five months. These have not been isolated cases, either; it seemed to be a general thing.
Another complaint that we hear very frequently is with respect to the treatment of the soldier in camp who happens to become sick. This has been reported to me personally not once, but several times; a soldier reports sick; he is sent to his battalion medical officer. Invariably he gets medicine
on duty, with practically no examination, and in some instances is fined 25 cents for reporting sick. When soldiers who have volunteered come home on leave and discuss these matters freely on the streets, there is not very much encouragement for the men whom we are trying to get to enlist voluntarily. That story is true; I have checked it, and I believe that situation should be remedied also.
There is still another matter with which we are concerned in Nova Scotia, at least; that is, the question of employment for men now unemployed. When they seek employment in the coal mining industry particularly, which is the basic industry of that province, the first question asked is whether they have medical certificates certifying that they are unfit for military service. If they do not have such certificates they are not taken on. On the other hand, a boy who is hired in that industry to-day is told definitely when he signs his employment card that he is hired for the duration of the war, and that when the war is over he will be relegated to the ranks of the unemployed. One hears it said quite freely on the street that if this is the programme of the government with regard to rehabilitation after the war, there is not much incentive for men to enlist voluntarily. In the first place, a man must be unfit for the army, and down there they construe that as equivalent to economic conscription. If a man is not fit for military service but is fit for employment, when he takes that employment he is told that it is only for the duration of the war.
There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, which I think works a great deal of injustice and hardship. A man enlists in Nova Scotia and is sent to Ontario. He has a family of five or six children, though his wife receives an allowance for only two children. Then the husband goes absent without leave for perhaps twenty-one days, and the wife's allowance is discontinued for perhaps two or three months, depending upon how long he was absent without leave and how long he was kept in detention after being caught. The family are not responsible for the actions of the man. When he goes into the army his sergeant-major is responsible for his discipline; and if the man gets away and commits infractions of military law, he should be punished, not his family. It is a sad spectacle to see a woman who has waited a month or two for her allowance, only to be notified by the department: "Your husband
The War-Air Services

was absent without leave, and as a result your allowance is discontinued," effective on such and such a date.

We have heard from every group in the house with respect to the granting of the cost of living bonus to old age pensioners and soldiers' dependents. In fact, to-night we have been privileged to hear all parties associating themselves with one another. That is a happy feature of to-night's discussion. But our associating with one another does not pay the bonus.
There is a principle in connection with the cost of living bonus which hon. members in their speeches to-night have not recognized. The hon. member for Trinity congratulated the Minister of Labour upon his humanitarian act in bringing down regulations whereby the cost of living bonus would be paid to wage-earners, and the hon. member urged that the minister do the same thing in connection with old age pensions. The principle is this: The government is not paying any cost of living bonus, but if it were to increase the old age pension or give a cost of living bonus to soldiers' dependents the government, that is the country or the taxpayers, would have to pay it or we would have to borrow the money. The cost of living bonus to wage-earners is paid by industry. The Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) can pass regulations covering the payment of a cost of living bonus to wage-earners, and yet he is not able to pass regulations in connection with bonuses to these other people.
I wish to associate myself and this group with what has been said. I think it will always be found that this group is willing to spend money. As a matter of fact, the social credit philosophy is one of spending, but not spending other people's money or the taxpayers' money or money which would have to be borrowed. We have another way of doing it, but I am not going into that tonight. I quite agree with the principle of a

I notice in the Ottawa Citizen this evening, on the front page, an item with the heading, "Reserve units get orders to recruit full complements." No doubt this is a move intended to further recruiting, but I am just a little afraid that certain difficulties will be encountered, in units especially that are not mobilized and are not associated directly with any unit serving overseas.
I happen to belong to such a unit, and in spite of the fact that we furnished one of the companies for the Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry Highlanders, the fact remains that it is a battalion which lacks the local colour and the local associations on which our unit was founded. We have many fine traditions, including, a brilliant record in the last war, at Cambrai, Amiens and other places; but we see units all round us being mobilized, while we are left, as it were, holding the bag. We have lost thirty officers to other units, as well as 150 riflemen and non-commissioned officers, and at present we are finding it difficult to get men to turn out for drill.
It might be interesting to the committee to hear the results I had in interviewing all the men in the company to which I happened to be attached, with a view of getting them to sign up for active service. This was when we were in camp at Connaught ranges last July. I am glad to say that very few men signified unwillingness to sign up for active service. Many wanted to join the air force immediately and have subsequently been enrolled in that branch of the service. Others signified their intention of joining the navy. By far the largest number said that they would sign up the minute the unit was mobilized for active service. This applies to officers and men alike. Since our return from camp, however, it has become increasingly difficult to get the men to turn out for drill, in spite of the fact that there is a fine of $5 in the civil court if they do not put in the thirty days which are required of them.
I would suggest, in this matter of trying to bring the reserve force units up to full war strength, that one company at least be composed of veterans of the last war, and that the age limit for these veterans be increased from forty-five to fifty, provided that they are in the proper medical category. I venture to say that if that were done, in a matter of weeks this company would be the smartest company in any reserve force unit; it would
be an inspiration and an incentive to the other companies; and in the event that they were needed for home defence, there would be none better to serve in that capacity. I know a great many returned men who on account of their age have been turned down, yet would make excellent recruits for a reserve force unit.
There is one other matter I wish to bring to the attention of the committee, namely, the number of officers from the last war who, since the outbreak of this war, have moved heaven and earth to get back into the service in some capacity. I have in mind two men, one of whom, especially, had a distinguished record in the last war and has vast military experience. In spite of trying every known means at his command, he has been systematically and consistently turned down. It seems to me that to leave a man of that type in civilian life is a great loss to the army. I feel sure that there are many others in the same position as this man, and I would heartily commend to the Department of National Defence that great consideration be given to utilizing this type of man, who wants to serve his country, who has the ability to serve his country, and above all, who has the experience.

Before we get too far away from this question of dependents' allowances, there is a little information I should appreciate having, and one or two observations I should like to make. My remarks apply particularly to the matter of the dependents' allowance as it applies to the parents of one who has enlisted. I have been informed on more than one occasion that there are regulations covering the payment of allowances to parents. On the other hand, I have been told from time to time that there are no such regulations. I would ask the minister, therefore, in the first place, if he would comment-I will put it in that way-upon the regulations regarding the payment of these dependents' allowances. In the second place, I should like to know whether such allowances are paid in cases where a condition of total incapacitation does not exist. I refer to this condition of total incapacitation by reason of the fact that in certain cases which have been brought to my attention the amount of allowance has been determined by the degree of incapacitation. I have in mind particularly one case wherein the dispute between the board and the individual had to do with whether this man was or was not 50 per cent disabled. It was finally decided that he was not 50 per cent disabled, and allowance was paid.
The War-Mr. Shaw

In the second case another applicant was turned down because he was not totally incapacitated. I do not particularly care about bringing these matters up on the floor of the house, but it seems that all other ways of securing information have failed as far as I am concerned.
About a year ago a certain man residing in my vicinity whose only son is in the service was rejected by the board because he was not totally incapacitated. After about a year he made application to have his case reexamined. When that application for reexamination was made, a certificate of a reliable physician was submitted. I was informed that a board would be set up to reexamine this applicant. According to the letter which I received from the applicant, a certain individual in the town concerned was communicated with by the dependents' allowance board and asked to set up a board to examine the applicant. Before, however, he had time to set up the board, the dependents' allowance board informed the applicant that a report had been received and that his claim had been rejected, the grounds being that he was not totally disabled from a physical point of view. Furthermore, it was stated that this man was capable of doing a day's work in the harvest field and therefore was capable of supporting himself. I should like to know exactly what steps are taken when a board is set up for the examination of a person who applies for dependents' allowance, and if the reports submitted to the dependents' allowance board have to be concurred in by all the members of the examining board. I intend submitting the particulars of this case to the minister, but I should like to have one or two comments.

There are other extraordinary cases. I have some correspondence regarding a young man aged fifteen who had enlisted without his father's consent. I wrote to the army asking some information about him, giving his number. The correspondence with the regiment lasted over two months, and finally I received one morning a letter stating that it was not possible to find that man. I was just reading that letter when I saw his face in the door of my office; he was coming to see me. I asked him, "What regiment do you belong to?" He mentioned the name of the regiment, and he gave me the number of his company. Therefore I could immediately dictate an answer to the letter telling me they did not know anything about him by saying

The War-Mr. Pouliot
that he was in my office and that the number I had given was the right number, and stating also what company he was in.
There was another young fellow, fifteen years old, who had enlisted without his father's consent. I sent a certificate of birth and a letter from the father saying the boy was too young to be in the army. He was in the ordnance. I wrote and wrote and wrote, and it was not possible to locate that man. The man existed. In the first place they knew nothing about the number; in the second case they knew the number fitted the man, but they did not know where the man was. I wondered whether he was a deserter, but he was not; only they did not know where he was. Finally, after two or three months, I discovered that he had been transferred from one unit to another and was in England. Then the army quite properly cabled to England to send him back here. I do not complain of headquarters with regard to that.
There are other extraordinary cases. There is one that I mentioned in the house in May or June of last year, which has been settled satisfactorily. It was most incredible, but the records are here in the department. The man has an English name although he does not speak much English, he speaks mostly French. He is a nice little fellow, a married man. First he was in Quebec city; then he was transferred to Camp Borden or Peterborough, or some camp in Ontario. I tried to get him a separation allowance; there was some correspondence, and I was told by one of the deputy ministers-the one who has resigned to enlist in the army-that this man was mentally unfit for the army. This soldier came home to visit a sick relative; while there, he had an attack of appendicitis. Following that, the next news I had was that he was a deserter. At the time he was arrested in Quebec city as a deserter he had in his pocket the original letter from the deputy minister stating that he was mentally unfit to remain in the army. I had to call Ottawa by long distance, and Ottawa had to call Quebec by long distance, in order to have this man released.
That is bad enough, but I read something worse in the Montreal Gazette, reprinted from the Toronto Telegram. For me there are no Jews or Gentiles, and I am quite eclectic in my appreciation of newspapers. This report stated that in an Ontario military camp there was high pressure when there was low pressure in other camps. The high pressure amounted to this: If a man signed his agreement to go overseas, he might enjoy leaves, passes and so on, and would be treated much better than the draftee who would not do so, though our
mobilization act is for the defence of Canada. Then there are certain commanding officers who want to have 100 per cent of their effective strength go across with them, and those who do not sign up to go are penalized by being made to do fatigue work until they do sign. Thus, while the others have a certain amount of freedom, and can enjoy leaves and passes, these men must wash the fioors and do that sort of work. It does not seem fair.
I should like to acknowledge my high appreciation of the kindness of the deputy minister and his secretary, who is just as efficient as the secretary of any executive-I need not mention names, but the minister knows of whom I speak-who have done their best to help me give all possible assistance to soldiers who are in trouble. That is the job we do. A friend of mine from across the floor mentioned that I had not been over there in the last war. I do not feel the need to speak of what has been done by anyone close to me; I do not like to boast of what has been done by others, but I am doing my very best in this war. I am trying to help those who want to enlist, by clearing away all possible difficulties in their way; but on the other hand I try to help obtain fair treatment for those who have a right to be exempted. It does not seem fair that men should be treated in the way they apparently are in our army.
I know of young men who have completed their courses at army schools, particularly at Vimy barracks, near Kingston. They were supposed to have learned trades, but instead were kept in the kitchen doing fatigue work, washing floors and so on. Some of these men were sent to Ottawa, but when they came here they were of no use; the officers here could not understand why men were sent here when they were not trained for the work they were supposed to do.
One day I was in Ottawa and needed some guidance with respect to certain correspondence. I telephoned the army, who told me to telephone national war services. I telephoned national war services, who told me to telephone the army. I said, "Well, I do not want to go from pillar to post; I want this information. The army directed me to you; now you return me to the army. I want to know where I must write." Then I called the army again; the army called the person who had drafted the regulations, and finally I was told that I must write to the registrar under national war services. In another case, with regard to an exemption that had been obtained by a certain man, I was directed by the army to get in touch with the chairman of the commission in Montreal, which I did, only to be told by this gentleman that it was none
The War-Mr. Pouliot

of his business. We do not know to whom we should address our requests, and that situation certainly should be cleared up.
There was something else I read, this time not in the Toronto Telegram but in the Ottawa Journal of September 24, stating that a census of the religious beliefs of the troops was being taken. I do not see how it is possible to do that when it is not possible to learn how many French-Canadians have enlisted in a certain regiment. All that information should be available.

Thank you. On the slope of Mount Royal, at the door of the new armouries, I noticed a bilingual invitation to young men to join the Black Watch, and this despite the fact that three French-Canadian regiments have not as yet been mobilized. These are the Joliet, St. Hyacinthe and Chateauguay regiments. Let me explain the point to my English-speaking colleagues. In the first place, French-Canadians were supposed to enlist in the old French-Canadian regiments, but if the doors of those regiments were not open to them, they had to swell the ranks of the Black Watch, the highlanders, and so on. Therefore these English regiments received credit for the enlistment of these French-Canadians. I do not think it is fair or just, and I had to bring to the attention of national defence headquarters the fact that French-Canadians sometimes were placed in regiments where the non-commissioned officers and officers did not speak a word of French, while they, the soldiers, did not speak a word of English. That is an absurd situation. They are alone and miserable in those circumstances. But when they are given an opportunity to be with men speaking their own language they are more at ease in military life.
I give credit to the deputy minister of national defence for having helped me transfer one of those boys who was stationed in the woods about twenty miles from Halifax. He was in an English-speaking unit, and was transferred to another one. Those are matters of fairness. It is a matter, not of religious or

racial prejudice, but merely one of giving to those boys the opportunity to serve under the best possible conditions.
Although I must praise highly the excellent work done by Protestant as well as Roman Catholic chaplains in the army, it is essential that those boys keep their religious beliefs, whatever they may be. One day I had a conversation with Mr. Hocken, who was at that time leading the Orangemen, and who spoke a great deal against Roman Catholics. He told me that it is much better for a young man to be a Roman Catholic than to be an atheist. Those young men should keep their beliefs, and should be given an opportunity to worship as they have been taught.
I have in my possession a letter sent to me by a priest at Pennfield Ridge. It states the case of a young man who complained of the way in which he was treated. He points out that a Protestant service was held in the camp in the morning, and that while a truck was standing idle, and there were several Roman Catholics present, those boys could not have the truck to travel only a few miles to attend mass. They were told to attend the religious services at the camp, and they were not permitted to go to their own church. In the letter only the first name of the soldier is given, but I shall be pleased to hand it to the minister. It was given to me by the parish priest.
I hope that those conditions will be changed, and that French-Canadians in the army will not be considered inferior. In Canada we are at times given an opportunity to hear fine, patriotic speeches. We must always understand that we are all brothers, and ready to do everything to help each other. But a French-Canadian should not be considered in the same category as the negroes of the southern United States. The sidewalk belongs to all. The way in which some French-Canadians are treated at Vimy barracks, Petawawa and even at Cornwall is shameful and unworthy of our country. I hope it will soon be corrected. I leave it to the Minister of National Defence to discuss it with the proper authorities. I know they are people of good will, and they are not always responsible for the wrong things that happen. But the finger must be pointed at them, so that the correction shall be made.
I should hope that between now and next spring Canadian defences would be improved. This is the time to do that, so that we may not be taken by surprise early next year. Some people may laugh at the suggestion; some may jeer, but let them remember that an ounce of caution is better than a pound of cure.

speechtext: My hon. friend misunderstands. I said that this body was set up as an ad hoc body, never as a permanent body, but I am very glad that the war expenditures committee confirms my judgment and makes it a permanent body. But my hon. friend has no right to blame anybody because it did not meet more frequently. It was not asked to meet. It did make a survey of all the military districts across Canada. From time to time it has been asked to make a survey. One such survey was made last week, as I have just told my hon. friend. If the war expenditures committee thinks this committee should be set up as a more permanent body, I am inclined to agree; I have no objection. As a matter of fact, I agreed with my hon. friend right from the start of the war. I felt that the Department of Pensions and National Health should do all the purchasing of drugs and medicines required because they have had twenty years of experience while the air force have none.

I do not want to get into any controversy over this matter. The member for Danforth is of the same opinion as the minister, and why? Because we find in that department men in uniform
-I have the highest regard and respect for them, and I know they are trying to do the very best they can-who have been drafted into this work in which they have had no training, men with sergeants' stripes accustomed to being warehousemen and shippers. They are gathering together equipment here in the National Grocers' building on York street, and they do not know the difference between an X-ray machine worth $5,000 and a bathtub worth $5. They are packing this stuff on trucks and shipping it out. They are men in uniform. They are doing the best they can, but they simply have not had the necessary experience. What is the result? I did not purpose putting this on the record, and when I do put it on I put it on because the minister has raised the point and with the idea of helping out a difficult situation.
With regard to equipment and the shipping of supplies across Canada by the medical services branch of the Department of National Defence, what do we find? First, with regard to the records, scores of thousands of dollars worth of goods bought, and properly so, to take care of these men, bought through means of indents made on the Department of Munitions and Supply, and properly so, and then brought into warehouses under the supervision of men in uniform, anxious to serve their country but inexperienced in the work that has been handed to them. The result was that the stockkeeping records on Kent street in July of this year showed thousands of dollars worth of goods supposed to be in store, and perhaps they were, supposed to be on the record as at the end of Canada's fiscal year ended March 31, 1941, and in July those records had not the official approval of the auditing service of the Department of National Defence. This is no charge, Mr. Chairman. This is a condition we are all anxious to remedy.

This work was sprung on them by reason of the war. I am commending this idea of an interdepartmental committee. These records were in lead-pencil figures. The balance on that ledger brought down as of March 31 was in lead pencil. Why were these figures not in ink? Because they had not been audited. In this muddle they said: "We will start off with a new bookkeeping system but will continue with the lead-pencil figures until such time as the audit is made for the financial year." They

The War-Mr. Harris (Danjorth)
carry on for April, May and June with a new set of books. In July the books are still not audited, and we asked the head of that service, "What about it?" The auditors were there in May, but the head of that service did not know whether these books had been audited up to the end of the fiscal year March 31, 1941. He admitted that frankly when he was asked what might be done to clear up the muddle and the mess they were in with regard to thousands and thousands of dollars worth of stock in medical stores for the whole of the army service. Mark you, Mr. Chairman, he had one system prior to March 31, and a new one after March 31. The deposition on the record says, "I think perhaps we should start a new system altogether." The result is that the books were not audited. What I am trying to say in my last sentence, is that the initiative which was inspired by that letter of December 5, 1940, should be carried through in those services.
